A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the brain regions that are active during bistable perception can be described by a dynamic model of brain connectivity.

the right anterior parietal cortex (aPC) is a key area involved in the resolution of perceptual ambiguity, and the strength of its interactions with the right posterior parietal cortex and the visual area V5/MT predicts the duration of perceptual dominance.

the neural dynamics of the brain can be described as the changes in connectivity strength among different cortical areas, and this connectivity strength can predict the individual differences in perceptual experience.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural dynamics of perceptual switches can explain individual differences in bistable perception, and that these dynamics can be captured by a predictive coding model.

we have identified a specific network that is involved in resolving the perceptual ambiguity associated with bistable perception, and that the dynamics of this network are related to the individual differences in the perceptual experience.
spontaneous perceptual reversals are not random but rather reflect a hierarchical predictive coding mechanism in which parietal and occipital regions are tightly coupled.
